TV Licence Scam Email UK: How to Spot a Fake

Criminals are sending convincing fake TV Licensing emails to UK households — here's how to spot them and protect yourself.

By Alex Bacsa · Published 2026-04-27 · Updated 2026-07-31 · 8 min read

Quick answer: TV Licensing sends genuine missed-payment emails, and its current Themis Recoveries trial sends emails about expired licences; some may contain links. A sender or link alone cannot prove the message is genuine. Do not use the email to verify itself: type tvlicensing.co.uk independently, check your licence or payment plan, and forward suspicious emails to report@phishing.gov.uk.
Key rule: verify through an official route you opened yourself, not the link, number, app, or payment details supplied by the suspicious message.

Being targeted right now? Do this

  1. Stop. Don’t pay, transfer money, or share passwords, PINs, or one-time codes.
  2. Contact your bank on the number on the back of your card if your money or details may be at risk.
  3. Use the right recovery route. Follow the payment, account and identity checklist; reporting differs in Scotland.

What a fake TV Licensing email looks like

A TV Licence scam email is a phishing message that copies TV Licensing's branding to get you to click a link and hand over card or personal details. An example of the style is: Your TV Licence payment was declined. To avoid a £1,000 fine, update your payment details within 24 hours: tvlicensing-update.example. The link opens a fake page designed to capture card details, online banking logins, or personal information.

The difficulty is that criminals choose the subjects TV Licensing itself writes about. TV Licensing sends genuine missed-payment emails, and its current Themis Recoveries trial contacts people whose licence has expired by letter, email and text. A failed-payment or expired-licence email is therefore not phishing simply because of what it is about, and a link inside it does not decide the question either. Settle it by checking your own licence and payment plan independently, not by reading the message more closely.

How to tell a genuine TV Licensing email from a fake one

Check your licence directly at tvlicensing.co.uk rather than treating a matching sender address as proof, because TV Licensing warns that scammers can spoof its genuine addresses. TV Licensing says its emails come from donotreply@tvlicensing.co.uk or donotreply@spp.tvlicensing.co.uk; TVL Pay app customers may also receive emails from noreply@paypoint.com, field-research emails may come from tvlfieldresearchteam@tvlicensing.co.uk, and its current Themis Recoveries trial uses mailing@themisglobal.co.uk for people whose licence has expired. If you have supplied your name, TV Licensing says it addresses you by title and surname. Its emails may include your name and/or part of your postcode.

TV Licensing says it only emails about payments if one has been missed, so check any unexpected payment claim independently — the Themis Recoveries trial is a separate route, used where a licence has expired.

Signs a TV Licensing email is a scam

  • The sender address is not one TV Licensing currently identifies for genuine payment, TVL Pay app, field-research, or Themis Recoveries trial emails — though a matching address is not proof the other way, because genuine addresses can be spoofed.
  • If you have supplied your name, a generic greeting such as "Dear Customer" or "Dear client" is a warning, because TV Licensing says it addresses you by title and surname. It may hold no name for you at all, so a generic greeting on its own is not proof either way.
  • It asks you to reply with bank details, or asks for personal details on a page you have not signed in to.
  • It threatens a fine or enforcement action unless you act within a short deadline.
  • It includes a licence or reference number you cannot match to your own account.

An unfamiliar, misspelled or lookalike address is a warning. TV Licensing currently lists tvlicensing.co.uk, tvl.co.uk, spp.tvlicensing.co.uk and 75plan.tvlicensing.co.uk as genuine, but visible link text and sender details can be faked. Do not use the message to verify itself: type tvlicensing.co.uk independently and check your licence or payment plan there.

How the scam works step by step

First, an email claims a payment, licence, or refund problem, using TV Licensing branding to look official. Second, urgency — a fine or a short deadline — pushes you to click without checking. Third, a fake page copying tvlicensing.co.uk asks for card, bank, or personal details before any sign-in. Fourth, criminals capture those details for card fraud, bank fraud, or identity theft, and may follow up by phone pretending to be TV Licensing or your bank.

Going to tvlicensing.co.uk yourself and checking your licence there, rather than trusting the email or its sender address (which can be spoofed), breaks the chain at the first step.

How to check a TV Licensing email safely

Do not click the link or reply with any details.

  • Check the sender address against the genuine addresses above, treating it as one signal only — scammers can spoof genuine TV Licensing addresses, so a matching sender is not proof.
  • Type tvlicensing.co.uk into your browser yourself, or sign in from an account you already have, rather than using the email's link.
  • For a missed payment, TV Licensing says it will not ask for card details until after you have signed in using your licence number, last name and postcode. Navigate to tvlicensing.co.uk independently and verify the same issue in your account rather than deciding from the sender or link alone.
  • The current licence fee is £180. A no-licence conviction can lead to a fine of up to £1,000. If a court has fined you, use the payment instructions from the court, not a link in a message claiming to be TV Licensing.
  • If in doubt, do nothing with the email and check your account directly instead.

If you clicked the link or shared details

If you entered card details, contact the card issuer immediately using the number on your card, tell them it was a scam, and ask them to secure or replace the card and check for transactions you do not recognise. Where an eligible card transaction was actually made or appears, ask which fraud or dispute route applies — chargeback only comes into play where such a transaction exists. If you sent a bank transfer, tell your bank the same day: our scam recovery checklist sets out the bank-transfer reimbursement rules and the conditions attached to them.

If you entered a password, change it through the real service and change any other account that reused it. If the page downloaded a file, installed an app or a configuration profile, asked for remote access, or the device has since behaved unusually, disconnect from the suspicious session and follow current NCSC guidance on responding to phishing and recovering a device.

If identity documents or personal information were exposed, review Cifas's current eligibility wording. Cifas says Protective Registration is only for people whose identities are at heightened risk. It places a warning flag that prompts extra checks on applications; it does not protect existing card transactions and is not insurance.

How to report a TV Licensing scam email (UK)

Forward the suspicious email to the NCSC at report@phishing.gov.uk, then delete it — TV Licensing's own scam-advice page directs readers to this same route for email. Do not reply to the sender, and do not call a number given in the message.

For an SMS, forward the message to 7726. For WhatsApp, Telegram or Signal, preserve the evidence and use the app's report and block tools; 7726 is not the in-app reporting route. If the same scam arrived as a letter, see our TV Licence Scam Letter UK: Spot a Fake Demand guide, and TV Licensing Scam Text UK: Spot a Fake Licence SMS covers the text version in detail.

If you lost money or shared sensitive information, report it to Report Fraud at reportfraud.police.uk or on 0300 123 2040 in England, Wales or Northern Ireland, or to Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland.

Frequently asked questions

Is confirmation@tvlicensing.co.uk a genuine TV Licensing address?

Treat it with caution. TV Licensing's currently identified senders are donotreply@tvlicensing.co.uk and donotreply@spp.tvlicensing.co.uk (plus noreply@paypoint.com for TVL Pay app customers, tvlfieldresearchteam@tvlicensing.co.uk for field research, and mailing@themisglobal.co.uk for its Themis Recoveries expired-licence trial). An address outside that list is a warning sign — but a matching address is not proof either, because genuine addresses can be spoofed. Don't click links; check your licence directly at tvlicensing.co.uk instead.

What is TV Licensing's official email address?

TV Licensing identifies donotreply@tvlicensing.co.uk and donotreply@spp.tvlicensing.co.uk as its genuine payment-email senders, with further genuine addresses for the TVL Pay app, field research, and its current Themis Recoveries trial. If you have supplied your name, TV Licensing says it addresses you by title and surname, and its emails may include your name and/or part of your postcode. Scammers can spoof genuine addresses, so always verify at tvlicensing.co.uk rather than relying on the sender alone.

Does TV Licensing really email people about missed payments?

Yes. TV Licensing sends genuine missed-payment emails, and its current Themis Recoveries trial contacts people whose licence has expired by letter, email and text, so a payment-problem email is not phishing by definition. TV Licensing says it only emails about payments if one has been missed. Check any unexpected claim by opening tvlicensing.co.uk independently rather than judging the message itself.

I clicked the link and entered my card details — what should I do?

Contact your card issuer immediately using the number on your card, explain it was a scam, and ask it to secure or replace the card and check for transactions you do not recognise; where a payment was made or appears, ask which fraud or dispute route applies. Change any password you entered, and any reused password, through the real service. If the page downloaded a file, installed an app or profile, or asked for remote access, follow current NCSC guidance. Then forward the original email to report@phishing.gov.uk, and use our scam recovery checklist for the account and identity steps.

How do I report a TV Licensing scam email?

Forward it to the NCSC at report@phishing.gov.uk. If you lost money or shared sensitive information, also report it to Report Fraud at reportfraud.police.uk or 0300 123 2040 in England, Wales or Northern Ireland, or to Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland.
